title: UK AI Safety Institute — Systemic Safety Assessment Protocol v2.0 — Q3 2026 Release
context: 2026-08-30 engine cycle — the UK AISI published version 2.0 of its Systemic Safety Assessment Protocol in Q3 2026, moving from a model-centric testing framework (v1.x) to a system-level safety assessment that evaluates the full deployment stack including data pipelines, orchestration layers, and human-in-the-loop interfaces; this is the protocol that operationalises the frontier testing regime and creates a procurement-gate mandate for any AI provider selling into UK government
body: The UK AI Safety Institute's Systemic Safety Assessment Protocol v2.0 (SSAP v2.0) is the methodological document that underpins the Institute's operational testing regime — think of v1.x as the research framework and v2.0 as the production-grade assessment protocol. Five changes define the v2.0 release. First, the unit of assessment shifts from 'model' to 'system': SSAP v2.0 evaluates the model plus its deployment scaffold — the data pre-processing pipeline, the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) configuration, the output filtering layer, and the human-in-the-loop interface — because the Institute's empirical work demonstrated that identical model weights can produce materially different safety profiles under different deployment architectures. Second, SSAP v2.0 introduces a mandatory 'containment declaration': the provider must state — in a signed, machine-readable format — what containment measures are in place (sandboxing, output filtering, rate-limiting, audit logging) and the Institute tests against the declared boundary. A provider that operates under a 'monitored containment' posture with audit-grade instrumentation satisfies this declaration by publishing a signed containment index; the Institute then tests whether the declared monitoring actually catches the misuse signals the protocol specifies. Third, SSAP v2.0 mandates cross-model interaction testing: if a provider deploys multiple models that can interact (e.g., a planning model calling a reasoning model, which calls a code-generation model), the assessment must test the interaction surface, not just each model in isolation. This is structurally similar to the swarm-verdict problem in multi-agent evaluation — the safety of the ensemble is not the sum of individual model safeties. Fourth, the protocol specifies evidence-chain requirements: every assessment finding must be linked to a specific model version, a specific deployment configuration, a specific evaluator identity, and a specific timestamp, with the entire chain hashed and signed. For a provider already maintaining signed benchmark manifests across a 14-axis governance board, this is a schema-alignment exercise — the same Ed25519-signed records that feed the board can be cross-walked to the SSAP v2.0 evidence schema. Fifth, SSAP v2.0 introduces a 'continuous reassessment trigger': if the provider updates the model weights, changes the deployment architecture, or if a new class of misuse vector is discovered, the assessment must be re-run within 30 days — not optional. This makes the signed, automated measurement pipeline that the Council of AI provides (nightly board regeneration, automated fix-record emission) a genuine operational advantage: instead of scrambling to reassess, the provider points the Institute at the continuously-updating signed benchmark stream. Practical steps: (a) map existing 14-axis board results to the SSAP v2.0 evidence schema. (b) Prepare a containment declaration in the Institute's prescribed machine-readable format, backed by a signed containment index. (c) Instrument cross-model interaction testing against the axes most relevant to your deployment architecture (swarm, detector-interop, machine-verif). (d) Automate the reassessment trigger so that any model or deployment change auto-queues a re-measurement and emits a signed record within the 30-day window.
